grammar.name: Absolute constructions
grammar.rule: This is a phrase with its own hidden subject, different from the subject of the main sentence. It adds background information without using a conjunction.
grammar.formula: Noun + participle (present/past), main clause.
grammar.example: Resources permitting, further research into food, agriculture and sustainability could yield significant long-term benefits.
grammar.tip: This is different from a participle clause: here, the noun is not the same as the subject of the main sentence.

grammar.name: Inversion after negative adverbials
grammar.rule: Some negative words can start a sentence: Seldom, Rarely, Never, No sooner...than, Little did..., Under no circumstances. When one of these words comes first, you swap the subject and the auxiliary verb, just like in a question.
grammar.formula: Negative adverbial + auxiliary + subject + main verb
grammar.example: Seldom have researchers observed such a rapid shift in food, agriculture and sustainability.
grammar.tip: Only swap the word order when the negative word is at the very start of the sentence. If it stays in its usual place in the middle, do not change the order.

grammar.name: Inversion in formal conditionals
grammar.rule: In formal writing, you can leave out the word 'if' in some conditional sentences. Instead, you start the clause with Had, Were or Should, and swap the subject and the verb.
grammar.formula: Had/Were/Should + subject + (not) + past participle / base form, ...
grammar.example: Had it not been for sustained investment, progress on food, agriculture and sustainability would have stalled entirely.
grammar.tip: Use this pattern only in formal writing. Never use 'if' and the inverted word order together in the same sentence.

grammar.name: Mandative subjunctive
grammar.rule: This is used after words like recommend, insist, essential, or vital — words that show a recommendation, a demand, or a necessity.
grammar.formula: Subject + suggest/recommend/insist + that + subject + base verb (no -s, no tense change)

grammar.tip: The verb after 'that' always stays in its base form. It never changes for person or tense: use 'be reviewed', not 'is reviewed' or 'was reviewed'.

grammar.name: Concession: despite/in spite of + noun/-ing vs. although + clause
grammar.rule: This shows a contrast, but the grammar after it depends on the connector you choose. Use a noun or an -ing phrase after 'despite'/'in spite of'. Use a full clause after 'although'/'even though'.
grammar.formula: Despite/In spite of + noun/-ing, clause. | Although/Even though + clause, clause.
grammar.example: Despite growing awareness of population growth and ageing societies, meaningful action has been slow to materialise.
grammar.tip: Never put a subject + verb clause right after 'despite' or 'in spite of'. This is one of the most common mistakes at B2 level.

grammar.rule: This moves a word or phrase to the start of a sentence. It usually connects back to the previous sentence or highlights an important idea.
grammar.formula: [Fronted adverbial/object], subject + verb...
grammar.example: Central to any serious discussion of population growth and ageing societies is the question of who ultimately bears responsibility.
grammar.tip: Use this mainly to connect your sentences clearly, not just to make your writing sound more varied.

grammar.name: Modal perfect for past speculation
grammar.rule: This shows how certain or uncertain you are about something in the past. You use a modal verb followed by 'have + past participle'.
grammar.formula: Subject + must/might/could/should + have + past participle
grammar.example: The delay in addressing privacy, surveillance and data must have resulted from competing political priorities.
grammar.tip: Choose the modal verb carefully. 'Must have' shows you are almost sure. 'Might have' or 'could have' shows it is just possible.

grammar.name: Appositive noun phrases
grammar.rule: This adds a noun phrase right after another noun, to explain or add detail about it, without using a separate relative clause.
grammar.formula: Noun, [appositive noun phrase], verb...
grammar.example: Concern over privacy, surveillance and data, once dismissed as a marginal issue, now dominates national policy debates.
grammar.tip: Put commas around this extra noun phrase, and keep it short so it does not make the sentence too heavy.

grammar.name: Correlative conjunctions (not only...but also)
grammar.rule: This connects two balanced ideas using a pair of linking words. When 'not only' starts the sentence, it triggers inversion in that clause.
grammar.formula: Not only + [inverted clause], but + subject + also + verb
grammar.example: Not only does privacy, surveillance and data affect the economy, but it also reshapes everyday social behaviour.
grammar.tip: Remember: if 'not only' is at the start of the sentence, you must invert the subject and verb. If it is in the middle, you do not.

grammar.name: Absolute constructions
grammar.rule: This is a phrase with its own hidden subject, different from the subject of the main sentence. It adds background information without using a conjunction.
grammar.formula: Noun + participle (present/past), main clause.
grammar.example: Resources permitting, further research into privacy, surveillance and data could yield significant long-term benefits.
grammar.tip: This is different from a participle clause: here, the noun is not the same as the subject of the main sentence.

grammar.name: Inversion after negative adverbials
grammar.rule: Some negative words can start a sentence: Seldom, Rarely, Never, No sooner...than, Little did..., Under no circumstances. When one of these words comes first, you swap the subject and the auxiliary verb, just like in a question.
grammar.formula: Negative adverbial + auxiliary + subject + main verb
grammar.example: Seldom have researchers observed such a rapid shift in privacy, surveillance and data.
grammar.tip: Only swap the word order when the negative word is at the very start of the sentence. If it stays in its usual place in the middle, do not change the order.

grammar.name: Inversion in formal conditionals
grammar.rule: In formal writing, you can leave out the word 'if' in some conditional sentences. Instead, you start the clause with Had, Were or Should, and swap the subject and the verb.
grammar.formula: Had/Were/Should + subject + (not) + past participle / base form, ...
grammar.example: Had it not been for sustained investment, progress on privacy, surveillance and data would have stalled entirely.
grammar.tip: Use this pattern only in formal writing. Never use 'if' and the inverted word order together in the same sentence.

grammar.name: It-cleft sentences
grammar.rule: An it-cleft sentence puts special focus on one part of a sentence — often the real cause, person, or reason.
grammar.formula: It + is/was + emphasised element + that/who + remainder of clause
grammar.example: It is precisely the lack of coordinated policy that undermines progress on privacy, surveillance and data.
grammar.tip: Make sure 'is' or 'was' matches the tense of the rest of the text. Do not use more than one it-cleft in the same paragraph.
